title: The Four-Month Project Doesn’t Exist Anymore
author: Dhwani Sagar
summary: Four months of building has been replaced by however long it takes you to figure out what you actually want to build. The hard part isn't execution anymore—it's creativity, uniqueness, and taste.
content: I keep thinking about how a project used to take three, four months to build.
When I was in college, major project could easily take three, four months to build.

And even with all four of those months, you still couldn’t really build everything from scratch. You’d have to cut things. Scope it down. Leave out things you actually wanted to build. If you were lucky, the final version would just about hold together and work the way you wanted.
That’s not really true anymore.

A lot of what you need is already out there. Whatever you want to build, however you want to build it, you can get pretty far, pretty quickly. The gap between “I have an idea” and “I have something working” has become much smaller.
Four months of building has, in some ways, been replaced by however long it takes you to figure out what you actually want to build.
And that’s great. But it also changes the game.
If everyone can make something that works, something functional, something that looks good, then working isn’t really the difficult part anymore.
The thing that stays apart, the little bridge between one project and another, is creativity and uniqueness.
Did you notice something that others didn’t? Did you think of something that someone else wouldn’t have thought to build? Is there something about your idea that makes it yours?
That’s the part you can’t really shortcut.
And honestly, I wish I could just walk into a classroom right now and see how this is actually playing out.
How are professors grading projects now? How are students doing assignments? What does “doing the work” even mean when so much of the work can be generated?
I’m curious about this because I graduated right as this shift was happening. I have one foot in the time before all of this and one foot in whatever this new version of things is.
I know what it was like when building something was the hard part.
I don’t really know what it feels like to be a student now, when building might be the easiest part.
And I think that’s where the bigger problem is.
The hard part isn’t building anymore. It’s judging.
When everything can look impressive, how do you tell a good idea from a bad one?
A mediocre idea and a great idea can both have a good-looking website, a working product, a nice case study, and a convincing presentation.
They can both look like they took months to make.
So how do you actually tell them apart?
I don’t think we have a good answer for that yet.
Not in classrooms. Not in portfolios. Not in hiring.
We’ve gotten really good at making things look finished. But we haven’t gotten equally good at figuring out whether the thing itself is actually good.
I think that’s the more interesting part of what’s happening right now.
It’s not really that AI can build things. We already know that.
The bigger change is that the difficult part has moved.
It used to be execution.
Now, I think, it’s creativity, uniqueness, and taste.
Having an idea worth building. Knowing which problem is actually worth solving. Looking at a hundred things that all look impressive and being able to tell which one is actually good.
I don’t have a clean answer for how academics, hiring, or portfolios should deal with this.
But I think that’s a much more interesting question to think about right now than what AI can or can’t build.

title: The Whimsical Brain in a Very Serious World
author: Dhwani Sagar
summary: Give me a blank canvas or a serious technical problem, and somehow a flower shows up. Whimsical thinking isn't the opposite of being bold—it's just my version of bold.
content: I can’t help but make things cute.
I’ve tried.

Give me a blank canvas, a serious idea, or some technical problem that’s supposed to look very serious, and somehow, somewhere in the process, a flower shows up. The colours become pastel. Something gets a little softer. Maybe there’s a tiny character that absolutely did not need to be there.

I don’t even plan it. I don’t look at something cool and think, “I should build that.” I look at it and think, “I want to make my own version of this. And it’s probably going to look nothing like yours.”
I’ve accepted that I’m one of those people.
## Whimsical doesn’t mean less bold
I think there’s a certain idea of what “bold” is supposed to look like in tech.
Sharp. Minimal. Serious.
Clean grids. Black and white. Dashboards. Big numbers. Things that look like they have very important places to be.
Sometimes that’s exactly what something needs. But I think there’s another kind of bold that doesn’t get talked about as much.

Making something soft when everything around you is trying to look serious. Putting a little personality into something that could have been completely plain. Making something cute without worrying that someone will think you aren’t taking the problem seriously.
That’s also a choice.
Give a whimsical person a serious problem and, somehow, a flower will be involved by the end of it.
I know, because I’ve done it enough times.
## I think this is why I like building things for feelings
I’ve started noticing that people who think like this tend to make things around imagination, memories, feelings, little rituals, and play.
Brainstorming tools. Mood boards. Memory keepers. Tiny things that don’t really “optimize” anything.
You end up building the thing you wish someone had made for you.
That’s basically what happened with one of my own projects.
I built a memory garden.
You post one photo a day, and slowly, it turns into a garden. Each month gets its own flower identity, so after a while you can actually see your days growing into something.
It’s soft. It’s slow. It doesn’t really do anything “productive.”
And that’s kind of the point.
It’s just there so ordinary days don’t disappear.
Not everyone is going to want that. Some people will look at a digital memory garden and go, “Okay… and?”
That’s fine.
I don’t think everything needs to be for everyone. Some ideas are meant to make sense to the person who was already looking for them.
## I didn’t realise this was a kind of brain
There are apps I’ve used for years without ever thinking about why I liked them.
Locket is one of those.
It’s basically a little widget that puts a photo from someone you love right on your home screen. When I first used it, I just thought it was cute.
That’s it.
But now that I’ve spent time actually building things, I look at something like Locket differently. I can see the decision behind it.
They could have made another photo-sharing app. They could have made the obvious version.
Instead, they made this tiny thing that feels like someone you love just sent you a little gift.
That kind of thing doesn't happen by accident.
Someone had to look at the obvious version and think, “Hmm. What if we made this a little more human?”
That’s a very specific kind of brain.
And I think I have it too.
I used to think that part of me was something I would eventually grow out of. Like once I got more serious about tech, I would stop making everything look a little too cute.
Apparently not.
## Maybe I don’t want to grow out of it
The more I build, the more I realise that not everyone sees things this way.
Give ten people the same problem and they’ll probably come up with ten different solutions. But somewhere in there, most of them will still make the functional thing.
The thing that works. The thing that makes sense.
And then there are a few people who can’t leave it alone.
They’ll add the little thing. Change the colour. Make the interaction slightly nicer. Put a flower somewhere for absolutely no reason.
And somehow, that’s the part you remember.
I don’t think whimsical thinking is the opposite of being bold.
I think it’s just my version of bold.
I like serious ideas. I like building things. I like solving real problems.
I just apparently can’t do any of that without sneaking a little softness into it.
And then?
I don’t think I want to.
If you also sneak flowers into serious problems, I’d love to hear what you’ve built.
